For a real symmetric cost matrix whose rank-width over $\mathbb{R}$ is at most $k$, we prove that every non-flat second-order stationary point of the factorized problem is globally optimal whenever the factorization rank is at least $2k$, independently of the matrix size.

item.title: Addendum to "Optimal Steering of a Linear Stochastic System to a Final Probability Distribution, Part II"
item.description: We hereby fill in a gap in an induction argument used in the proof of a theorem on state-covariance controllability of linear stochastic systems in an earlier paper by the authors. The mathematical statement is true. The missing point in the proof concerns the assertion that, in the canonical single-input case, the control can be assigned arbitrary endpoint values. We amend the argument by proving a slightly stronger induction statement that permits arbitrary finite endpoint jets of the control. An independent approach to homogeneous state-covariance controllability was provided in a paper by Abdelgalil and Georgiou (2025) as a corollary of strong controllability results on $\GLp(n,\mathbb R)$, and shown herein that it extends to the case of additive noise as well.

item.title: Incremental Stability of Gradient Flows under Generalized Polyak-Łojasiewicz Inequalities and Its Implications for General Systems
item.description: Gradient flows of twice continuously differentiable strongly convex and convex objectives are, respectively, incrementally exponentially stable and non-expansive in the Euclidean metric. In this work, we investigate to what extent these properties extend to nonconvex objectives satisfying generalized Polyak-Łojasiewicz inequalities. For objectives with a unique minimizer, we establish conditions under which the gradient flow is contracting in a state-dependent Riemannian metric and incrementally exponentially stable. For objectives with nonunique minimizers, we generalize the non-expansivity of convex objectives to incremental stability for more general nonconvex objectives. We focus on incremental stability due to its implication to convergence to equilibrium points; when paired with a Lyapunov function it implies pointwise convergence to a minimizer and continuity of the endpoint map. Along the way, we derive new structural results for incrementally stable nonlinear systems and extend the analysis to Heavy-Ball and Dynamical Inertial Newton flows.

item.title: Fast and Accurate Hydro Unit Commitment
item.description: We introduce a fast novel algorithm to commit hydro-generators. We show that our algorithm can commit 56 generators for 200 days 10,000 times faster than Hexaly, the leading commercial solver for scheduling problems, without sacrificing solution quality. Our method can commit 1792 generators for an entire year in approximately 20 seconds on commodity hardware. Hexaly is unable to solve problems of this size in reasonable time. We attain this runtime improvement by introducing a greedy-heuristic tailored for hydro units. We provide a direction for a possible proof that the error our solver makes decreases with the problem size. This is supported by our experimental results. We prove that our solver's runtime scales log-linearly in the number of generators and time periods.

item.title: Learning Stabilizing Latent Feedback Controllers via Multi-Step Backward Losses
item.description: Can learned latent dynamics models support the design of feedback controllers that provably stabilize the original system? For linear time-invariant systems, we show that learning linear autoencoders and latent dynamics with multi-step prediction-reconstruction losses $\unicode{x2014}$ which we term "backward losses" as they encourage latent trajectories to reconstruct full state trajectories $\unicode{x2014}$ provably recovers the structure needed for stabilization. Specifically, a sufficiently long reconstruction horizon ensures that a minimum ${H}_\infty$-norm controller designed using the learned latent model stabilizes the original system through output-feedback via the corresponding encoder, provided the latent dimension is large enough to capture all non-stable modes of the underlying system. We also show why both reconstruction and a multi-step horizon are essential: forward prediction losses that require only low prediction error along latent trajectories admit global loss minimizers that discard unstable modes regardless of horizon length, while single-step reconstruction losses can yield latent models whose stabilizing controllers fail to stabilize the original system. Finally, experiments on a non-linear flexible-arm system illustrate the practical implications of our results for learning non-linear autoencoders and latent dynamics.

item.title: Immersed Boundary Electrodiffusion in the Wasserstein Gradient Flow Formalism: Global Well-Posedness, Non-Equilibrium Thermodynamics, and Singular Asymptotics
item.description: We introduce a unified optimal transport framework for the Immersed Boundary (IB) electrodiffusion active pump model. By representing membrane chemical potential barriers and active pump potentials via smoothed Eulerian kernels ($Ψ_w, \mathcal{H}_w$), we formulate the passive dynamics as an $L^2$-Wasserstein ($W_2$) gradient flow coupled to non-conservative active pushing fields representing ATP-driven $3:2$ $\text{Na}^+/\text{K}^+$ exchangers. We establish global weak existence of solutions to the continuous Poisson--Nernst--Planck--IB system via a split-step Jordan--Kinderlehrer--Otto (JKO) variational scheme, backed by Calderón--Zygmund bounds for non-local Poisson drift and $H^3(\mathbb{S}^1)$ interface regularity under Stokes flow. We prove the continuous Rayleighian energy balance and establish exponential $W_2$-stability of Non-Equilibrium Steady States (NESS) under a quantitative Bakry--Émery curvature threshold. Furthermore, we analyze the dual singular limits of kernel smoothing width $w \to 0$ and dimensionless Debye length $g = λ_D / L \to 0$. We establish the precise asymptotic regime connecting regularized and sharp models, prove the $Γ$-convergence of regularized energy functionals, derive distributional interface flux jump conditions, and resolve $O(λ_D)$ Debye space-charge boundary layers to confirm bulk electroneutrality.

item.title: Scientist Mothers Working in Childcare Deserts Are Less Likely to Attain Tenure
item.description: Childcare shortages have limited families' access to quality care, with consequences for children's development and parents' careers. We link two decades of childcare supply data to longitudinal surveys of U.S. scientists. We find workplace childcare deserts are widespread: more than half of scientists at universities and research institutions work in deserts, where supply falls significantly short of demand. We further find mothers working in deserts are less likely to attain tenure. They are also more likely to move to industry and part-time positions. Reduced work time partly accounts for the tenure association but other reasons remain. Expanding childcare availability near workplaces may help retain scientific talent.

item.title: Neural Network Methods in the 2BSDE Formalism for Solving the High-Dimensional Black--Scholes Equation with Transaction Costs
item.description: A 2BSDE system is written down for a $(D+1)$-dimensional Black--Scholes partial differential equation (PDE) with the Leland transaction cost model which incorporates the sign of the curvature. The 2BSDE system takes input from the ``speed'' (derivative of the curvature). This system is solved using a single ResNet neural network which learns both the solution to the PDE as well as the degrees of freedom in the curvature matrix. The network is used to learn the price of derivatives such as call options and butterfly spreads on geometric baskets for $D=10,100$ achieving a time-averaged RMSE of less than $0.1$ in each case.

item.title: CuPIQP: A Batched and Differentiable QP Solver on GPUs for Robot Learning and Control
item.description: Quadratic programs (QPs) are fundamental building blocks of many robotic tasks such as inverse kinematics, whole-body control, and model predictive control. Extending these methods to large-scale robot learning and control requires solving many QPs concurrently and, for end-to-end learning, differentiating through their solutions. Efficient batched optimization is therefore essential to bringing established model-based methods into GPU-based robotics pipelines. We present \textsc{cuPIQP}, a batched and differentiable QP solver on GPUs based on a proximal interior-point method, with unified support for dense, sparse, and multistage problems. The solver exploits parallelism across independent QPs and their internal structure while preserving per-problem numerical updates and termination decisions. Benchmarks with up to 16384 QPs per batch demonstrate solve-time speedups of up to $18.8\times$ over \textsc{Moreau} and $4.26\times$ over eight-core \textsc{PIQP}. In an end-to-end learning task, \textsc{cuPIQP} accelerates training by $4.6\times$ over \textsc{QPAX} and $7.8\times$ over \textsc{Moreau}. By reducing the computational cost, \textsc{cuPIQP} provides efficient, reusable infrastructure for integrating model-based optimization into large-scale robot learning and control.

item.title: When can Optimally Trained Transformers Achieve Near-Lossless Token Prediction for non-Markovian Data?
item.description: There exists little mathematical theory explaining why Transformer architectures are empirically successful even for non-Markovian data. To this end, this paper studies next-token prediction via stochastic optimal control theoretically trained Transformers for such sources, where we consider either stationary and ergodic non-Markovian sources or those which are hidden Markov models of some finite order (possibly non-stationary). In either case, we first obtain error bounds via finite models with finite window approximations. For stationary ergodic sources, the resulting error is bounded by an entropy gap; for $N$th order Markovian sources, it decays at an exponential rate $α^{\lfloor M/N\rfloor}$, where $M$ is the window length and $α$ is determined by filter stability (and the Dobrushin coefficients of the transition and measurement kernels). We then construct a Transformer of depth $M+1$, one head per layer, realizing the truncated filter, and we optimally train it with stochastic control developed in earlier work, which rigorously returns a near optimal Transformer. In particular, we show that for a non-Markovian source, either under stationarity and ergodicity for general models or under filter stability for hidden Markov models, an optimally trained Transformer has arbitrarily small performance error with increasing context length, data, and approximation refinement. Numerical studies accompany the theory.

item.title: Box-Cone Representations of Bound-Factor RLT Constraints in Semidefinite Relaxations
item.description: Linear inequalities can generate large constraint systems in semidefinite relaxations of binary quadratic programs, making the quadratic subproblems of splitting methods expensive to solve. We develop a box-cone representation of bound-factor reformulation-linearization technique (RLT) constraints in semidefinite relaxations of binary quadratic programs. These constraints arise by multiplying each original linear inequality by every binary variable and its complement and linearizing the resulting products. Our key observation is that all products generated by one inequality share a common slack and admit an exact representation in the standard cone over the unit box. This box-cone representation processes the inequalities through independent explicit projections, without introducing a separate nonnegative slack for each scalar RLT inequality. We illustrate the computational use of the representation within standard two-block alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). The resulting subproblems require linear solves with a reusable factorization and explicit cone projections, without enlarging the semidefinite matrix. Experiments on 257 binary quadratic programs compare this implementation with SDPNAL+. A second application groups Max-Cut triangle inequalities into box cones and uses the resulting bounds within an existing branch-and-bound framework. Tests on 220 graphs show competitive performance with MADAM using only triangle cuts. Together, these applications illustrate the representation's usefulness as a building block for first-order methods.

item.title: String-averaging bargaining in solidarity cooperative games
item.description: We consider the situation that the grand set of all players, in a cooperative game in characteristic function form with a nonempty core, consists of recognizable subsets of players. The underlying assumption is that the players of each subset have something in common between themselves which is not shared by the players of other subsets. For example, the members of these subsets are distinguishable by their nationalities or by their geographic locations or by some other market-related economic or social property. In addition to the agreement of all players to play the game to reach a point in the core, the members of each subset want to steer the iterative orbit of the bargaining process to a point in the core that will reflect the strength of their solidarity within their subset. This is why we call such subsets solidarity sets. The solidarity means that players of a solidarity set are willing to participate in coalitions that include only members of their solidarity set and are not willing to participate in coalitions of other solidarity sets. The question is how can such a game be played? Is there an iterative bargaining scheme that will generate a sequence of payoffs that converges to a point in the core which reflects the solidarity of the members of the solidarity sets? We propose bargaining schemes that allow the members of each solidarity set to perform, independently from other solidarity sets and, therefore, simultaneously in time, a full but finite sweep of intercoalitional collaboration. Then the end-points of all these sweeps are combined into a single payoff vector via a convex combination wherein the coefficients of the convex combination may reflect some a priori knowledge about the relative strengths of the different solidarity sets. These bargaining schemes are applied to a new type of cooperative game that we call solidarity cooperative game (SCG).

item.title: Stochastic Linesearch Methods for Stochastic Variational Inequality Problems: Parameter-Free Schemes and Non-Monotone Variants
item.description: Much of the existing convergence guarantees and rate statements for stochastic variational inequality (SVI) problems are limited to stochastic approximation schemes that employ constant or diminishing steplength sequences bounded by some reciprocal of the Lipschitz constant $L$ of the map. This requires both knowing such constants and may lead to debilitatingly small steplengths, afflicting the scheme with potentially poor performance. We propose a parameter-free stochastic extragradient method with periodically restarted linesearch (\textbf{SEG-LS}) for solving pseudomonotone and monotone SVI problems. The resulting stepsize sequence is neither monotone nor requires prior knowledge of the Lipschitz constant $L$. We show that the iteration and sample complexities for computing a point whose residual has norm at most $ε$ in expectation are $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-2})$ and $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-4})$, respectively. These results improve to $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-1})$ and $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-2})$ in the monotone setting. In addition, we propose a periodically restarted biased stochastic linesearch method (\textbf{B-SLAM}) for solving non-monotone SVIs under strict copositivity. The resulting iteration and sample complexities are $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-2})$ and $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-4})$, respectively. Preliminary numerics support these findings and display promise.

item.title: Stochastic and Noisy Oracles in Smooth Continuous Optimization
item.description: We review models of inexact computational oracles in smooth continuous optimization and their implications for the convergence, computational complexity, and attainable accuracy of optimization algorithms. We adopt a framework in which zeroth-,first-, and second-order oracles are characterized by quantitative error bounds and may accept additional control parameters that influence both their accuracy and computational cost. We introduce deterministic and stochastic oracle models and illustrate their properties through a variety of examples, including finite-difference approximations, stochastic gradients, and randomized derivative estimators. Particular attention is given to the distinction between absolute and relative errors, bias and variance, and stochastic function evaluations with independent or coupled randomness. A central theme of the review is the use of common analytical tools to recover and compare convergence and complexity guarantees under different oracle models. For deterministic and stochastic first-order methods, we show how a general descent inequality leads to complexity bounds under various assumptions on the objective function and all proposed oracle models. In the stochastic setting, we develop bounds on expected stopping times and the accuracy that can be guaranteed under different oracle conditions. We also examine the total computational complexity of algorithms relying on specific oracle constructions and briefly review models of inexact second- order information and their use in optimization algorithms.

item.title: Local Budget Benefits, Population Commitment, and Solver Performance: A DGO Case Study with Controlled DE Transfer
item.description: An evaluated candidate can improve a local search step, alter the population used by later steps, and affect a solver's final result. We distinguish these three questions using Da Gou Gun Optimization (DGO), a population optimizer designed for this study. Its JQ100 configuration evaluates an interpolation candidate during a two-sided probe. We define local budget value, population commitment effects and complete-policy performance, and give an exact example in which a locally better commitment leads to a worse continuation. Short-horizon matched comparisons favor interpolation on eligible quadratic states. Paired continuations yield mixed effect estimates, with primary group intervals spanning zero. Complete-policy comparisons favor JQ100 over the tested classical references in aggregate; a matched-start comparison has favorable means but intervals spanning parity. On 24 boxed BBOB functions, target-truncated geometric-mean error ratios favor JQ100 over the tested classical policies and favor L-SHADE and CMA-ES over JQ100 under the stated initialization and stopping rules. Local evaluation gains, commitment effects and solver competitiveness therefore require separate comparisons.

item.title: Quantum Vehicle Routing Problem: a smart initialization strategy for ill-conditioned optimization landscapes
item.description: With the expansion of complex transport infrastructure, new paths for linking different destinations have emerged, allowing the definition of multiple routes. The introduction of new roads may also lead to disruptions in traffic flow. This problem can be generalized into a special case of VRP, which aims to find the optimal route for a fleet of vehicles within a network of destinations. Finding solutions to this problem requires an exponential number of operations, hindering the ability of exact solvers to deal with large instances, which must therefore be tackled using heuristics, often leading to suboptimal results. Quantum-based algorithms may allow us to find exact solutions in polynomial time with high probability, offering a potential future alternative to classical solvers and in this work, we focus on the QAOA. Our novel contributions are a parameter-initialization strategy that improves the convergence probability and the integration of the subtour constraints directly into the optimization without using additional qubits by employing an approximation of exponential equality constraints. We believe that our results pave the way for effectively solving instances of VRP using quantum-based solutions, leveraging the space-efficient problem encoding and our initialization strategy, which limits the effect of barren-plateau under random parameter initialization.

item.title: Turnpike Properties for Exploratory Stochastic Linear-Quadratic Optimal Control with Indefinite Cost Functionals
item.description: Continuous-time exploratory stochastic control provides a stochastic control framework for the exploration--exploitation trade-off in reinforcement learning. In this paper, we study the long-time behavior of finite-horizon exploratory stochastic linear-quadratic (LQ) optimal control problems as the time horizon $T\to\infty$, and establish so-called turnpike properties for such problems. In the finite-horizon setting, we derive a feedback representation of the exploratory stochastic LQ problem and analyze its long-time structure. We formulate an exploratory static distribution optimization problem analogous to the classical static optimization problem and identify the corresponding static reference object. We prove a turnpike property for the optimal state process relative to a stochastic reference process, as well as a Wasserstein turnpike property for the optimal control distribution. In addition to the exploratory control formulation, another key feature of our results is that, by introducing a joint coercivity condition, we allow the cost functional to be indefinite and the controlled state system to be merely stabilizable. Consequently, the derived turnpike property is novel even within the classical stochastic LQ control framework.

item.title: Koopman--Lyapunov and Koopman--Riccati Controller Synthesis
item.description: While the Koopman operator-based lifted representations of nonlinear autonomous and controlled systems have been well covered in the literature, the direct controller synthesis problem largely remains open. As the controlled system is generally a bilinear (instead of fully linear) Koopman model, controller synthesis appears to lose the linear--quadratic structures of the classical Lyapunov and Riccati methods for finite-dimensional linear systems. However, in infinite dimensions, bilinearity in the feature map should be merely artifactual and hence reducible to linearity in principle. In this work, by considering the operator semigroups in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space with a linear--Sobolev kernel and utilizing the Yosida approximation of their generators, the synthesis problems of a stabilizing controller and an input-unconstrained optimal controller can be formulated as an operator Lyapunov inequality and an operator Riccati equation, respectively. These formulations recover the desirable linear--quadratic structures, and hence, with sample data, they are solvable efficiently in analogous ways to usual linear systems by semidefinite programming solvers and Kleinman iterations, respectively. In addition to proving control performance bounds dependent on the sampling denseness and Yosida regularization, through numerical comparison to linearized LQR, bilinear EDMD-based synthesis, nonlinear MPC, and Koopman MPC methods on numerical models and process control examples, this work demonstrates the proposed Koopman--Riccati synthesis as a computationally efficient approach to obtain a near-optimal state-feedback control law.

item.title: Algebraic Vector Fields of Connected Semi-simple Matrix Groups are 3-generated
item.description: We show that the Lie algebra of algebraic vector fields for any connected, semi-simple matrix group over $\mathbb{F}$, for $\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C}$, can be generated by three $\mathbb{F}$-complete algebraic vector fields.

item.title: DistFlow and Its Conic Relaxation: Regularity, Monotonicity, and Hybrid Exactness via Graph Decomposition
item.description: Classical exactness conditions for conic relaxations of the DistFlow model rely, among other assumptions, either on all nodal injections being adjustable or on a network-wide path condition. In practice, these conditions may not hold uniformly across a feeder: controllable distributed energy resources (DERs) sit at some buses and fixed loads at others, while reverse flows from DER-rich regions can violate the path condition. This paper certifies exactness region by region and composes the regional certificates, accounting for perturbations that propagate downstream through voltages. We first introduce a subtree voltage stability region, in which the network and all compatible subtrees remain regular. Within it, two endpoint sign conditions, one relaxing the nonnegative-flow assumption and one implied by the classical path condition, yield monotone responses of voltages, currents, and losses to root voltages. Using duality, the implicit function theorem, and sign properties of inverse sensitivity matrices, we recast both classical arguments as individual sign certificates on branch multipliers. This turns exactness into a branchwise property that can be certified region by region. A partition rule then splits the network into dispatchable and passive subtrees, and a hybrid certificate combines their local conditions into exactness of the full-network relaxation, under additional operating-limit and objective conditions. In particular, placing controllable DERs at both ends of a branch with large reverse flow exempts that branch from the passive sign conditions.

item.title: Stochastic Mirror Descent under Dependent Observations
item.description: We study the non-asymptotic convergence of Stochastic Mirror Descent (SMD) algorithm when the noisy first-order oracle is driven by dependent observations. Departing from the classical i.i.d. assumption underlying most existing guarantees, we introduce a flexible ``forgetting" condition that accommodates geometrically or polynomially dependent sequences. Under this condition we derive explicit finite-sample accuracy bounds for the averaged SMD iterates, recovering the classical $O(1/T)$ and $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ rates in the large- and small-initial-error regimes. We instantiate the general framework on two applications: high-dimensional linear regression with dependent regressors and nonparametric estimation of the drift function of a functional autoregressive model.

item.title: Sparse descent subspace-Newton thresholding algorithm for sparse optimization problems
item.description: In this paper, we propose a sparse descent direction derived from the Newton direction within a low-dimensional subspace for sparse optimization problems. Building upon this direction and incorporating hard thresholding and orthogonal projection, we develop a novel algorithm termed the sparse descent subspace-Newton thresholding (SDSNT) algorithm. We further establish its global convergence under the restricted isometry property $δ_{3k}\leq \sqrt{3/20}$ of the measurement matrix. Numerical experiments on random sparse vector recovery and audio signal reconstruction reveal that SDSNT achieves comparable performance to several state-of-the-art algorithms. Notably, relative to most of them, it delivers superior recovery at high sparsity levels and improved efficiency at low sparsity levels.

item.title: RapidDOC: Riccati-Preconditioned Implicit Differentiation for Differentiable Optimal Control under Operator Mismatch
item.description: Differentiable optimal control embeds constrained optimization problems in data-driven pipelines by differentiating their optimality conditions and propagating task-loss gradients to model or objective parameters. A key observation is that forward optimization and backward sensitivity computation involve related stage-structured linear systems, making reuse of forward factorization information natural. However, direct reuse is generally invalid, because differences in linearization, barrier terms, regularization, and curvature can create a mismatch between the retained forward operator and the target operator defining the derivative. We therefore propose RapidDOC, a factorization-reuse method that leaves the target adjoint equation unchanged. The retained cache produces a candidate adjoint and, when its target residual exceeds the prescribed tolerance, serves as a fixed right preconditioner for GMRES. A cache-action error operator characterizes directional exactness, the preconditioned iteration, and the relation between target residual and outer-gradient error. An ablation on three constrained robotic OCPs shows that the proposed method achieves lower backward time than both target-system refactorization and a no-reuse iterative method, demonstrating the computational benefit of reusing the retained forward factorizations. Across open- and closed-loop parameter-learning experiments, the proposed method achieves learning performance comparable to the baselines, while yielding the lowest open-loop backward time on all three tasks and reducing total closed-loop solver-call time by 40.5-83.1% relative to the fastest competing method. Finally, deploying the learned controller on a physical vehicle reduces the median figure-eight tracking RMSE from 22.75 to 6.09 cm, demonstrating its potential for hardware deployment.

item.title: Region-Preserving Accelerated Gradient Methods for Geodesically Convex Optimization
item.description: Accelerated Riemannian optimization methods often require a priori assumptions that their iterates remain in a region where geometric bounds hold. We develop a parameterized inertial dynamical system and an explicit accelerated gradient method for smooth geodesically convex optimization on Riemannian manifolds with locally bounded sectional curvature. Our setting allows both positive and negative curvature without requiring completeness of the ambient manifold. Starting from a curvature-corrected continuous model, we construct the discrete updates by eliminating indefinite cross terms in the Lyapunov energy difference and derive verifiable conditions for a fixed step size. The resulting energy analysis establishes preservation of the initial geodesic ball without assuming iterate containment in advance. We further establish accelerated convergence rates for both geodesically convex and strongly geodesically convex objectives, without requiring restarts.

item.title: Riemannian Optimization on Unknown Manifolds via Stochastic Proximal Refinement
item.description: We study Riemannian optimization on an unknown manifold accessed only through feasible samples. The central challenge is to turn feasible samples into optimization steps, i.e., the samples are drawn from the unknown feasible manifold, but do not directly provide the tangent spaces, projections, or retractions required by classic Riemannian methods. Moreover, regions with low objective values may be sparsely represented in the data, so directly sampling from a distribution fitted to these observations can require many draws to find better feasible solutions. We introduce Proximal Refinement on Implicit Smooth Manifolds (PRISM), which turns feasible-sample access into an iterative optimization procedure by repeatedly sampling an objective-aware proximal distribution conditioned on the current iterate. Theoretically, we show that PRISM recovers the effect of Riemannian-gradient refinement, leading to provable objective descent, feasibility (manifold adherence), and convergence toward first-order stationarity. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through synthetic experiments illustrating its geometric properties and applications to data-driven building control and diverse real world optimization tasks, highlighting its potential as a general framework for data-driven optimization across scientific and engineering domains.

item.title: A Dual-Guided Column-Generation-Based Matheuristic for Integrated Railroad Blocking
item.description: Integrated railroad blocking is a central planning problem in freight railway operations, which requires coordinated decisions on block design, blocking sequences, and block routing. We propose a dual-guided column-generation-based matheuristic (DG-CGM) that uses linear programming (LP) dual information to identify promising transportation paths and incorporates them into restricted mixed-integer programs to improve feasible solutions. Starting from an initial plan built by construction, DG-CGM alternates destroy and local repair with path generation, which uses dual prices from restricted LPs of a Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation to identify promising transportation paths. When local improvements continue to stagnate, we further apply joint repair to combine alternatives across demand groups. To address the coupling between logical and physical path pricing, we introduce a joint reduced cost that eliminates path-specific dual variables from pricing, enabling more efficient column identification through exact labeling algorithms. We evaluate the performance of DG-CGM on both generated instances and real-world cases. On 150 generated instances with 50-150 nodes, DG-CGM achieves the optimal cost on 89 of the 91 instances solved to proven optimality by Gurobi, with a geometric mean runtime equal to 5.2% of that for Gurobi and a mean relative cost reduction of 3.4%. On six full-scale scenarios derived from the 2026 INFORMS Railway Applications Section competition data, each with 47,193 nodes, DG-CGM obtains feasible solutions within two hours that serve 95.9%-99.6% of the requested freight volume, providing practical blocking plans for large-scale railway operations. The code, instances, and computational results are publicly available at https://github.com/Zhengzhong-You/IRBP.

item.title: Infeasible Momentum Orthogonalized Methods for Optimization on the Stiefel Manifold
item.description: We study deterministic and stochastic optimization over the Stiefel manifold, explicitly allowing iterates to deviate from the manifold rather than enforcing feasibility via retraction at each step. We introduce Landom, a Landing-type method that constructs momentum in the relative-gradient direction, maps this update to its compact polar factor, and combines the resulting tangential step with a step along the negative gradient of the orthogonality penalty to improve feasibility. Under operator-to-nuclear smoothness, Landom achieves an $O(T^{-1/2})$ bound on the averaged nuclear norm of the relative gradient with exact gradients, and an $O(T^{-1/4})$ bound in expectation with stochastic momentum, bounded variance, and a fixed batch size. Our analysis also provides explicit pathwise bounds on the orthogonality residual, including its dependence on the step size and initial infeasibility. To address the coupling between objective and feasibility correction in Landom, we further propose Landom+, a two-timescale variant in which the tangential and normal step sizes are decoupled. By keeping the normal step size fixed, Landom+ achieves tighter control over the orthogonality residual following an initial transient while maintaining the respective convergence rates for stationarity. Numerical experiments across a range of applications illustrate that the proposed algorithms remain competitive with established manifold optimization approaches.

item.title: Physically Constrained Kinematic Calibration for High-Precision Robotic Needle Guidance
item.description: Percutaneous needle insertion is a common practice in minimally invasive procedures whose clinical success depends on accurate needle placement. However, achieving the necessary precision is a challenge for manual operators. Robotic assistance can improve targeting accuracy and reduce operator dependence, but residual millimeter-scale errors persist because nominal kinematic models do not fully represent the physical manipulator. This paper presents a robust bound-constrained kinematic calibration method designed to improve positional accuracy for a 6-Degree-of-Freedom (6-DoF) robotic needle-guidance manipulator. The approach uses physically plausible parameter ranges to regularize a compact 19-parameter geometric identification model. By treating these bounds as active optimization constraints rather than mere numerical safeguards, the framework effectively mitigates parameter coupling and overfitting, ensuring highly stable parameter identification. In simulation, the proposed method reduced end-effector Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) from 3.422 mm to 0.690 mm (a 79.8% improvement). In benchtop hardware experiments, the calibrated model achieved sub-millimeter validation accuracy, including 0.865 mm RMSE in experimental trajectory validation and 0.610 mm RMSE in a coordinate-lattice verification task. These results demonstrate that physically constrained kinematic calibration can enhance robotic needle-targeting accuracy, establishing a high-precision foundation for future clinical applications.

item.title: Bellman semigroups. Quarante ans d'après
item.description: We revisit the relation between discrete- and continuous-time stationary dynamic optimization, using both the Bellman and Hamiltonian descriptions. We study the problem of embedding discrete Bellman--Lax--Oleinik operators and the associated Hamiltonian cascades into continuous-time dynamics. Rather subtle obstructions to such embeddings emerge even under the most natural assumptions.

item.title: Stability of ideal Nash equilibrium points in generalized multi-criteria games, interval-valued games, and existence in single-leader--multi-follower problems
item.description: We study the stability of ideal Nash equilibria in generalized multi-criteria games, in which each player's vector-valued payoff is ordered by a closed cone and the feasible strategy sets depend on the other players' strategies. Under compactness and continuity assumptions, the ideal Nash equilibrium correspondence is upper semicontinuous on the class of games admitting an ideal equilibrium. Our main result does not require the ordering cones to be convex or pointed. In fact, the ideal equilibria are exactly the common equilibria of associated scalar games when all the cones are convex. As consequences of our results, the stability of interval-valued games is derived and existence theorems for single-leader-multi-follower problems are proved for both optimistic and pessimistic sense.

item.title: Improving the Optimization Landscape of Matrix Completion with $ε$-close Surrogates
item.description: Non-convex optimization is central to machine learning and AI, yet unlike its convex counterpart, it still lacks a general and principled framework. In this work, we try to highlight the importance of combining noisy perturbations with over-parametrization mathematically under the classic setting of matrix completion (MC). Matrix completion is an important non-convex recovery problem in which only a subset of a matrix's entries is observed, and the remaining entries must be recovered using low-rank constraints. This problem is notoriously difficult because observations are limited. However, we show that by injecting $ε$-level perturbations into the nullspace of the observation mask, we can construct noisy matrix sensing surrogates whose solutions remain $\mathcal{O}(ε)$-close to the ground truth with valid restricted isometry property (RIP) constants. The existence of RIP further enables powerful tensor frameworks to be applied with theoretical guarantees. This approach reflects a broader empirical trend in which stochasticity or noise improves the curvature of the optimization landscape, allowing over-parameterized (a.k.a large) models to better separate signal from noise. Assuming each matrix entry is observed independently, we establish quantitative recovery guarantees without explicit requirements on sampling rate or incoherence, and discuss how such assumptions can further strengthen our results.

item.title: Improved Approximation Guarantees for Periodic-Review Stochastic Inventory Control
item.description: In periodic-review stochastic inventory control, replenishment policies must balance holding and backlogging costs while responding to uncertain demands and evolving forecasts that may be arbitrarily correlated and nonstationary. In this general information setting, Levi, P{á}l, Roundy, and Shmoys (Mathematics of Operations Research 2007) established that the fully adaptive optimum can be approximated within factor $2$, which had remained the best-known performance guarantee since then. Their marginal cost accounting and dual-balancing framework made this comparison possible without computing optimal decisions across future trajectories, opening a broad research program on approximation algorithms for stochastic inventory systems. We break this long-standing barrier for periodic-review stochastic inventory control, showing how to compete against the fully adaptive benchmark within factor $\frac{ e }{ e-1 } \approx 1.582$ while retaining general demand correlations and evolving forecasts. We attain these advances by discovering a structural connection between marginal inventory accounting and weighted stopping problems, where each unit's conditional holding charge forms a supermartingale, while postponing its order incurs a history-dependent backlog charge. To leverage the random thresholding approach of Ma and Tzamos (ICML 2023) in this context, we develop a potential-function analysis, leading to an $\frac{ e }{ e-1 }$-approximation with respect to any unit's stopping problem. Subsequently, our common-threshold policy coordinates these marginal decisions into a global replenishment policy without additional loss.

item.title: A bounded degree SDSOS hierarchy for solving SPLD polynomial programs
item.description: A polynomial optimization problem is said to have an SPLD structure if the polynomials defining its objective and constraints admit decompositions into separable and nonseparable parts, with the maximum degree of the separable parts exceeding that of the nonseparable parts. In this paper, we propose a bounded degree SDSOS hierarchy for globally solving a class of such problems. We establish the asymptotic convergence of this hierarchy over compact feasible sets and provide a sufficient condition for its finite convergence. Numerical experiments compare the proposed hierarchy with the BSDSOS hierarchy (Chuong et al. in J. Global Optim., 75(4):885-919, 2019).

item.title: Robust Principal Component Analysis via $\ell_0$ Alternating Minimization
item.description: Robust principal component analysis concerns the recovery of a low-rank matrix $Z$ and a sparse matrix $S$ from their observed sum $D = Z + S$. In this paper, we study this recovery problem under an $\ell_0$ sparsity penalty and a rank constraint on the low-rank component. By exploiting the entrywise separable structure of the sparse subproblem, we obtain an exact closed-form solution via hard thresholding with box clipping, avoiding the shrinkage bias of $\ell_1$-based methods. The low-rank subproblem is solved by truncated SVD. We prove block-coordinate convergence of the resulting alternating minimization scheme, establish uniqueness of block minimizers under non-degeneracy and singular value gap conditions, establish local linear convergence under a contraction condition on the Fréchet derivative of the truncated SVD operator restricted to the sparse support, and provide a second-order optimality analysis via the Riemannian Hessian. Experiments on synthetic data, images, and video show that the proposed algorithm outperforms the existing convex and nonconvex algorithms, most notably in support recovery and in the accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

item.title: Direct and indirect operator learning strategies for parametric optimal control problems
item.description: This paper focuses on the use of learning nonlinear operators via Deep Operator Networks (DeepONets) for approximating the solutions of optimal control problems. We study two operator learning strategies, namely, indirect and direct, both based on DeepONets, for parametric families of optimal control problems where the same problem must be solved many times for different initial data, different parameters, different cost function weights, and different bounds defining the set of the admissible controls. In the indirect strategy two DeepONets approximate the solution operators of the state and adjoint systems, and their predictions are used inside iterative projected gradient algorithms for finding the optimal control. In the direct strategy, a single DeepONet approximates the operator that maps directly to the optimal control generated by a reference solver; consequently, a new control is obtained through a single evaluation of the network. In order to analyze the computational cost, the efficiency, the speed and the accuracy of the learning strategies, we consider an optimal control problem related to an ordinary differential system that describes the temporal evolution of the glioblastoma growth subject to therapeutic interventions. For this specific optimal control problem we propose a discretize-then-optimize strategy, based on an implicit-explicit finite difference method, and then, we develop several numerical experiments in order to compare the two DeepONet learning strategies for this problem. The proposed operator learning DeepONet strategies can be adapted to approximate large classes of optimal control problems related to diverse differential systems.

item.title: Distributed Grid Search for Hyperparameter Tuning
item.description: The performance of many distributed optimization algorithms over peer-to-peer networks strongly depends on the choice of their hyperparameters. However, existing selection rules often require global quantities, yield conservative choices, or are tied to specific algorithms and hyperparameters. We propose Distributed Grid Search (D-GS), a consensus-based search method that evaluates and selects hyperparameter configurations across the network, requiring only the ability to run the tuned algorithm and evaluate local gradients. We also propose a zoom-in variant, Distributed Zoom Grid Search (D-ZGS), which improves empirical performance at a reduced cost. We prove that both methods terminate in finite time with all agents holding the same hyperparameter configuration, and quantify the (sub)optimality of this configuration. Numerical experiments on linear and logistic regression show that D-GS closely matches a centralized reference and that tuning and deployment cost a fraction of deploying algorithms with hyperparameters tuned using theoretical results.

item.title: A Parallel Heuristic for the Fixed Cardinality Binary Quadratic Program
item.description: The Fixed Cardinality Binary Quadratic Program (FCBQP) is an optimization problem that requires a prescribed number of variables to take the value 1. We propose a parallel CPU-based heuristic that combines impact-based variable selection, tabu search, guided restarts, and a shared elite pool. Computational experiments on 342 benchmark instances from the maximum dispersion problem, k-clique problem, and minimum graph bisection problem show that the new algorithm is competitive and can reach best-known or reference values on instances with more than 20000 variables within one minute.

item.title: A complete analytical characterization of optimal collision-free motion for two robots
item.description: Collision-free motion planning for multi-agent robotic systems remains an active research area because of the complexity of coordinating robot trajectories, with applications ranging from coordinated drone shows to autonomous operations on land, in the air, and on water. Importantly, the analytical difficulty of nonconvex collision-avoidance constraints has so far driven the development of exclusively numerical methods. We derive a complete analytical characterization of the optimal trajectories for two robots that start and end at rest, under double-integrator dynamics and a squared-acceleration objective. We prove that these trajectories belong to eight distinct contact families and determine which family applies for each configuration of initial and final positions. We analyze the geometrical properties of the optimal trajectories, provide a numerical algorithm for computing them, and discuss how these insights may improve the performance of existing numerical trajectory optimizers.

item.title: Polynomially Solvable Cases of the Quadratic Binary Optimization Problem with a Fixed Cardinality Constraint
item.description: Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) problems and their variant with a fixed cardinality constraint are both well-known NP-hard problems. While certain structural properties of the cost matrix can make some QUBO instances solvable in polynomial time, this advantage typically disappears once a cardinality constraint is added. In this work, we investigate specific structural conditions on the cost matrix under which the constrained version-quadratic binary optimization with a fixed cardinality-remains tractable.

item.title: Underdamped Stochastic Optimal Transport with Landauer boundary conditions: machine learning and analytical solution
item.description: Finding optimal transport protocols for underdamped stochastic processes is a difficult yet important problem in control theory. In this paper we develop a direct method, based on machine learning, to find the optimal solution of the problem in the presence of non-linear boundary conditions, including those modelling the Landauer bit-erasure problem. The dynamics is steered from a single-peak to a double-peak distribution in position space, by only acting on a controllable external potential. The problem is highly non-linear, and analytical solutions are not available in general. We benchmark our numerical results with a perturbative expansion, which is expected to hold in a suitable overdamped limit.

item.title: Distributed Zeroth-Order Composite Finite-Sum Optimization via Incremental Variance Reduction
item.description: We study decentralized composite finite-sum optimization over a fixed connected undirected network, where agents access local component functions through function evaluations and share a possibly nonsmooth convex regularizer. In this setting, standard two-point gradient estimators can retain nonvanishing variance at a solution, complicating their integration with gradient tracking. We propose Distributed Zeroth-Order Incremental Variance Reduction (Distributed ZIVR), which combines incrementally updated component-gradient estimates with a proximal gradient-tracking scheme. The method admits an implementation using a constant number of function evaluations per agent at every iteration, without intermittent full-component or full-coordinate refreshes. For convex smooth component functions and strongly convex local averages, we establish linear convergence up to a controllable finite-difference error. With the finite-difference radius chosen for the target accuracy, Chebyshev-accelerated mixing yields a per-agent oracle complexity of $\widetilde{O}(d(m+κ)\log(1/ε))$ for expected squared solution error $ε$, where $d$ is the dimension, $m$ is the number of components per agent, and $κ$ is the condition number. This matches the centralized ZIVR oracle bound, while the communication bound has only an inverse square-root dependence on the network spectral gap. Experiments on logistic and robust regression demonstrate rapid reduction of solution and consensus errors.

item.title: Boundary stabilization of a moving interface in a 2 x 2 weakly hyperbolic system of balance laws: application to continuous sedimentation
item.description: We design a boundary feedback for the level of the sediment bed of a continuous settler and prove that it exponentially stabilizes the linearized closed loop under a small-gain condition. The unit is modeled by a 2 x 2 system of balance laws in which the bed surface, the interface, is not a smooth part of the solution but a moving shock between a weakly hyperbolic free-settling zone and a strictly hyperbolic compression zone. We describe it by the Rankine-Hugoniot relations and map the problem onto a fixed domain. Moreover, we prove local well-posedness with a continuation criterion given by a single margin function. Then we linearize the system near an equilibrium. The linearization couples a dissipative distributed layer to one scalar, the interface position, whose equation does not contain the control. We solve this by infinitedimensional forwarding: a Sylvester kernel cancels the interface trace and isolates the interface pole, and a proportional feedback then sets its decay rate. Every hypothesis is verified on an illustrative example, a laboratory-scale continuous settler containing a bed of compact polystyrene beads.

item.title: Chance-Constrained Inspection Viewpoint Sequencing for On-Orbit Servicing via Safe Reinforcement Learning
item.description: Autonomous inspection of a target spacecraft is typically the initial step in on-orbit servicing. Planning close-proximity observation viewpoints involves a complex combinatorial problem constrained by coverage, fuel, and safety considerations. This paper models the viewpoint selection as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP) and applies Proximal Policy Optimization with Lagrangian relaxation to solve it. The system combines a high-level planner, which sequences camera viewpoints on an observation sphere around the target, with a low-level model that assesses each transfer using the Clohessy--Wiltshire (CW) equations for relative motion. The deterministic constraints on single-impulse reachability and $Δv$ cap are enforced directly on the action set. Safety margins are affected by navigation and manoeuvre errors, making the actual clearance stochastic. To address this, a chance constraint on the realised trajectory is implemented, with a Lagrangian multiplier governed by PID control to adapt the penalty during training. The approach is tested on a Galileo-class navigation satellite in medium Earth orbit, modelled as a point cloud where visibility from each viewpoint considers field-of-view and line-of-sight occlusion. Across various risk budgets, the trained policy maintains the keep-out violation rate within the specified limit, achieving coverage close to its maximum and staying within the mission $Δv$ budget. Compared to the usual practice of applying a fixed margin to the keep-out radius and planning deterministically, the chance-constrained policy attains less than half the violation rate at comparable coverage. This makes the collision risk an explicit design parameter, eliminating the need for re-tuning per case. The learned policy selects a viewpoint without the repeated Monte Carlo risk estimates required by a greedy, chance-constrained planner at every decision point.

item.title: Risk-Sensitive Mission Planning for Multi-Target On-Orbit Inspection via Distributional Reinforcement Learning
item.description: Multi-target on-orbit servicing missions require planning tools that can adapt to evolving operational conditions while accounting for the outcome variability inherent to safety-critical spaceflight. This paper presents an adaptive planning approach for multi-target servicing campaigns in low Earth orbit and applies it to inspection missions flown by a low-thrust servicer. The approach is based on Distributional Reinforcement Learning, which learns the full distribution of mission returns and thereby supports explicit risk-sensitive decision-making at each planning step. Specifically, a Quantile-Regression Deep Q-Network (QR-DQN) agent selects which target to inspect next by jointly considering the expectation and the variance of the predicted return through a mean-variance criterion. The mission environment models circular orbits with a spread in inclination and uses Edelbaum's combined-manoeuvre low-thrust transfer estimates. The observation comprises the orbital elements, the visit history, the observed risk state of each target and the remaining mission-time budget. The risk state of each target changes stochastically during the campaign, making the outcome of an inspection uncertain and creating operationally meaningful distinctions between risk-neutral and risk-averse planning strategies. Because the mission-time budget generally admits only a subset of the candidate targets, the planner must also select which targets to inspect. Numerical experiments on scenarios with five target satellites show that one risk-aversion weight moves the policy across a range of mean return and return variance, over an unchanged environment and reward. Risk-averse agents reduce the variance of the episodic return by approximately one half relative to risk-neutral agents and lower the probability of a mission loss, at a cost in mean return. To validate the learned policies, the efficient frontier, which gives the highest mean return attainable at each level of return variance, is computed exactly by enumerating the admissible visit orders. At equal variance, the learned policies lie close to this frontier in mean return, and the risk-averse policies have a lower probability of a mission loss than the frontier policies.

item.title: Overcoming the Representational Limitations of Amplitude Encoding for Quantum Neural Networks
item.description: Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) offer a framework for learning functions from classical data, but their expressive power depends critically on how inputs are encoded into quantum states. Angle encoding can require resources that scale with the number of features, whereas amplitude encoding represents $d$ features using only $\mathcal{O}(\log_2 d)$ qubits. This compactness comes at a representational cost: normalization makes conventional amplitude encoding invariant to nonzero real rescaling of the input, up to an unobservable global phase. We show that this invariance induces an exact, architecture-independent restriction on the resulting hypothesis class. No downstream quantum circuit can distinguish inputs differing by nonzero real scaling. We develop a general condition under which deterministic preprocessing can remove this ambiguity and show that nonlinearity alone is insufficient. Based on this analysis, we introduce a fixed nonlinear feature map that provably distinguishes all real inputs under subsequent amplitude encoding, without adding trainable parameters and while retaining logarithmic qubit scaling. We evaluate the resulting QNN on three canonical classification benchmarks and a nonlinear synthetic dataset against conventional amplitude and angle encoding, as well as a classical neural network. Across these tasks, the proposed encoding consistently improves classification accuracy over both quantum encoding baselines by 21$-$44 %. Our results establish normalization-induced scale invariance as a concrete representational bottleneck of amplitude encoding and demonstrate that it can be removed while preserving a compact quantum representation, marking a step toward quantum models capable of capturing arbitrary relationships in classical data.

item.title: Integrating Low-Thrust Transfer Dynamics into POMDP Planning for On-Orbit Servicing
item.description: Recent developments in both high-thrust (HT) and low-thrust (LT) propulsion technologies broaden design options for on-orbit servicing (OOS) missions. However, incorporating LT transfers into OOS mission planning requires accounting for the trade-off between prescribed transfer duration and propellant consumption. Multi-servicing, multi-transfer OOS mission planning is inherently sequential and requires adaptive planning tools that account for propulsion-dependent transfer durations and mass-dependent propellant consumption. Thus, transfer dynamics must be integrated into mission planning and scheduling to increase flexibility and adaptability. In addition, the planning is often done with imperfect information about the system's state and stochastic service demands. This paper focuses on modeling orbital transfers, particularly LT transfers, within a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) framework for OOS mission planning. To enable offline policy computation, the transfer model must provide explicit state transitions and rewards for all admissible actions. The state space is therefore augmented with the servicing vehicle's remaining propellant to enable consistent mass updates. HT transfers are modeled using a precomputed transfer matrix that maps each transfer to the time of flight and propellant consumed. LT transfers are represented using an analytical GEO phasing model with prescribed transfer-duration alternatives. For each alternative, the model calculates propellant consumption and maneuver feasibility as functions of the required phase change and the current servicing-vehicle mass. The proposed modeling approach is evaluated on simplified OOS planning scenarios using circular phasing with HT and LT propulsion. The resulting POMDPs are solved using the Successive Approximations of the Reachable Space under Optimal Policies (SARSOP) algorithm, and the policies obtained under HT and LT are compared. This comparison provides a quantitative assessment of the feasibility and operational impact of LT options, particularly regarding the potential role of advanced electric propulsion in future servicing architectures.

item.title: Safety Verification for Voltage Control in Inverter Dominated Radial Distribution Networks under Actuator and Sensor Adversarial Attacks
item.description: This paper develops a safety verification framework for inverter-based radial distribution networks under sensor and actuator attacks. Each customer is equipped with a droop-based controller to regulate its voltage within a desirable bound of a reference, i.e., to achieve safety. In our setting, attacks and disturbances enter the droop-based controllers, while actuator attacks corrupt the reactive power injected into the network. Consequently, invariance of the controller state alone does not guarantee compliance with inverter capacities or customer voltage limits. To address this challenge, we derive conditions to guarantee that the reactive power state remains inside a predefined ellipsoid, while at the same time ensuring that the attacked reactive power injections and customer voltages respect predetermined operating limits that hold uniformly for the entire predefined ellipsoid. Together, these conditions guarantee safety under all admissible disturbances and state-dependent sensor and actuator attacks. Finally, we express the resulting containment condition as a linear matrix inequality (LMI) feasibility problem. A five-customer radial network based on the CIGRE benchmark corroborates our theoretical developments in simulations.

item.title: Variance Reduction for Decentralized Stochastic Optimization with Multiple Local Updates
item.description: Multiple local updates are widely used in decentralized optimization to enhance communication efficiency, often in conjunction with stochastic gradients when exact gradient computation is costly. However, such algorithms generally converge only to a neighborhood of the optimum, whose size depends on the stepsize and the variance of gradient noise. Variance reduction has been incorporated into ADMM-based methods to achieve exact convergence in expectation, but their stepsizes typically scale inversely with both the square root of the network size and the cube of the number of local updates, leading to slow convergence as the network size or the number of local updates increases. In this paper, we propose a novel primal-dual-based decentralized optimization algorithm that integrates variance reduction with multiple local updates, with a stepsize independent of the network size and inversely proportional to the number of local updates (rather than its cube), thereby enabling significantly larger stepsizes and faster convergence. Moreover, to the best of our knowledge, we establish the first linear convergence guarantee in expectation for decentralized optimization with multiple local updates under stochastic gradients in the strongly convex setting. Beyond the theoretical guarantee, the proposed method exchanges only one variable per round, halving the communication cost compared with gradient-tracking-based methods. Numerical experiments further demonstrate its advantages in convergence speed and accuracy.

item.title: On Universal Minkowski Classes of Polytopes: Theory and Applications
item.description: This paper establishes the existence, in every dimension, of universal Minkowski classes of configuration-constrained polytopes, with direct applications to set-theoretic control. For any prescribed accuracy, such a class contains an approximation of every compact convex set to that accuracy and admits a jointly affine parameterization of facets and vertices. The construction is explicit and relies on a combinatorial averaging procedure that produces minimal configuration enclosures. In control, these polytopic templates enable convex reformulations of otherwise non-convex problems, including invariant-set computation and control Lyapunov function design. Tutorial examples illustrate both the geometric construction and its control applications.

item.title: Near-Optimal Second-Order Convex Finite-Sum Optimization under Individual Smoothness
item.description: We study the stochastic second-order oracle complexity of solving smooth convex finite-sum optimization with $n$ components. Very recently, Tsedenov \& Kovalev (2026) showed that the minimax optimal complexity under averaged smoothness and convexity is $\tildeΘ(n + n^{6/7} ε^{-2/7})$ by establishing nearly matching upper and lower bounds. In this paper, we show that individual smoothness and convexity provably enable further acceleration, where the lower complexity bound is $Ω(n+ n^{5/7} ε^{-2/7})$ under this stronger assumption. Then, by establishing a novel second-order self-bounding inequality, we design a new Taylor-corrected lazy Newton method, which can lead to a better complexity of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n + n^{5/7} ε^{-2/7})$ by applying the optimal Monteiro-Svaiter acceleration, matching our lower bound up to only logarithmic factors.

item.title: Exact Theory and Optimal Stepsizes for Stochastic Gradient Descent in Smooth Convex Minimization
item.description: This work considers the design of stepsize schedules for stochastic gradient descent in smooth convex optimization. Throughout, we assume that gradient noise is conditionally zero-mean with bounded variance. Among problems with dimension $d\geq N+1$, we provide an exact worst-case analysis of the expected suboptimality of stochastic gradient descent's final iterate. Our analysis applies to any (potentially nonconstant) schedule of $N$ stepsizes in $[0,1.5]^N$. Here, exact means that we provide a matching objective function and noise distributions where our guarantee is attained. Whenever the variance bound is at least $Ω(1/\sqrt{N})$, our theory provides the minimax optimal stepsize schedule for stochastic gradient descent and proves its uniqueness. These optimal stepsizes monotonically decrease, ruling out any accelerations in expected final suboptimality from fixed fractal schedules observed in the deterministic case.

item.title: The Quartic Gap Between Quantum and Dequantized Algorithms for Linear Algebra Is Tight
item.description: Quantum algorithms for linear algebra that access a matrix $A$ through quantum random access memory (QRAM) prepare quantum states proportional to the solutions of linear systems and related problems. Dequantized classical algorithms, when given sampling and query access to $A$, return sampling and query access to an approximate solution. Both kinds of algorithms use a number of queries that is polynomial in the normalized Frobenius norm $ρ=\|A\|_F/\|A\|$ and does not directly depend on the dimension. For linear systems at fixed condition number and accuracy, quantum algorithms use $\widetilde O(ρ)$ queries, whereas the best dequantized algorithms use $\widetilde O(ρ^4)$. We prove that this quartic gap is tight in the worst case, up to a logarithmic factor. For every constant $κ_0>1$, we construct dense linear systems with condition number at most $κ_0$ for which sampling from the solution within a sufficiently small constant total variation distance requires $Ω(ρ^4/\logρ)$ classical queries but only $Θ(ρ)$ quantum queries. The same separation holds, for errors below smaller thresholds, for positive-definite systems, least squares, ridge regression, matrix powers and square roots, imaginary-time and real-time Hamiltonian evolution, and sampling from the top principal component. Our results therefore show that many quantum algorithms for linear algebra, achieve a near-quartic speedup in the worst case, over classical algorithms with sampling and query access. All of these classical lower bounds follow from the same framework, which is based on a lower bound for sampling from distributions that depend on a fixed set of Fourier coefficients of an unknown Boolean function.

item.title: Stochastic Rayleigh-Ritz Ascent: Global Linear Convergence under a Spectral Gap
item.description: We consider the adjoint-free random-plane iteration algorithm for finding the top eigenvector of a matrix proposed in (SIAM J. Matrix Anal. Appl. 47 (2026), 1349-1374). Unlike standard methods such as the power method or gradient descent, the above algorithm lacked linear convergence guarantees in the presence of a spectral gap. In this paper, we establish explicit spectral-gap-dependent global linear convergence rates in expectation, providing quantitative guarantees for the empirically observed convergence.

item.title: Cost-Aware Stopping for Freeze-Thaw Bayesian Optimization: When Does One-Step Lookahead Suffice?
item.description: Freeze-thaw Bayesian optimization (BO) evaluates candidates in resumable increments but usually stops at a budget or convergence test. We maximize a budget-free utility, the best observed score minus a cost per increment, with a one-step lookahead: advance the candidate with the largest expected improvement (EI) under a fixed surrogate, and stop once no EI exceeds the cost. This rule, EI stopping, never falls below stopping immediately in expected utility, yet it can stop too early. We construct a certificate, a lower bound on the value of two-step lookahead, that proves such a stop premature, and repeating this correction never lowers expected utility under the surrogate. Under the surrogate, EI stops are premature on average at low costs and lose little at high costs. On three hyperparameter optimization benchmarks, a pre-registered test finds EI stopping noninferior to the correction in most high-cost settings, while the correction gains at low costs on two of the three; more information sharing in the surrogate raises EI stopping's utility. On the surrogates of two published methods, EI stopping trades lower scores for fewer training increments. EI stopping is a simple cost-aware reference whose utility depends on the surrogate.

item.title: Regret-Optimal Wasserstein-Robust Linear Regression
item.description: Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) minimizes worst-case risk under distributional uncertainty, but its decisions can be suboptimal in terms of their excess risk, or regret. We study this gap for multivariate least-squares regression, assuming that the observed source law and unknown target law differ by an adversarial 2-Wasserstein perturbation of size $\varepsilon$. We first identify the asymptotic complexity of robust decision-making in the $\varepsilon \to 0$ limit, characterized by a problem-specific condition number $κ$. Here, a wide spectrum of simple algorithms, including DRO, achieve the instance-optimal rate of $O(κ\varepsilon^2)$. For fixed $\varepsilon > 0$, we prove that DRO still achieves the minimax rate if the problem has bounded residual effective rank. On the other hand, we identify significant failure modes where DRO is provably suboptimal by dimension-dependent factors. Fortunately, we prove that two alternative procedures, minimax regret optimization (MRO) and spectral-norm regularization (SNR), attain the minimax rate. We derive an exact convex reformulation of MRO and an accelerated proximal algorithm for SNR, along with high-probability finite-sample guarantees. We support these theoretical results with numerical experiments separating the performance of MRO and SNR from DRO.
